Scottish Terrier Grooming and Health-Question Planning

Plan Scottish Terrier ownership around coat care and hand-stripping, an independent temperament, dental attention, and a worksheet you fill with local quotes.

Published: 2026-10-20Sources checked: 3Educational planning guide

With a Scottish Terrier, the recurring commitments are coat maintenance and a stubborn, independent streak, so the smart planning is about a realistic grooming schedule and the health questions to raise with breeders and your vet.

An independent terrier by design

The American Kennel Club describes the Scottish Terrier as an independent, confident companion of high spirits with an almost-human dignity, and notes that its terrier persistence earned the nickname the Diehard. That persistence is charming and also means a Scottie may decide your recall is optional. Plan for patient, motivating training rather than expecting instant compliance.

The core answer for a prospective owner is that a Scottie rewards owners who enjoy a spirited, self-possessed small dog and can commit to steady grooming. This guide gives a coat-care schedule and health-question list, and pairs with our five-year ownership cost framework.

It helps to reframe the independence as a feature rather than a flaw. A Scottie is not a dog that lives to please every request, and owners who expect that dynamic can feel frustrated. Owners who appreciate a dog with opinions, on the other hand, tend to find the breed delightful. The training goal is cooperation, not blind obedience, and that shapes everything from how you motivate the dog to how much you rely on management, such as leashes and fences, in situations where a firm recall cannot be assumed.

The coat: clipping versus hand-stripping

A Scottie's harsh double coat needs regular upkeep, and you will choose between clipping and hand-stripping. Hand-stripping preserves coat texture but takes skill and time, while clipping is simpler but softens the coat. Either way, budget for regular professional sessions or the tools and hours to do it yourself. Our hand-stripping cost guide and grooming salon interview guide help you compare options and quote it honestly.

  • Between grooms: Regular brushing to prevent mats, plus beard and furnishings cleaning.
  • Nails and ears: Routine trimming and checks on a set schedule.
  • Decide the method early: It changes both your budget and your time commitment.

Whichever method you choose, consistency beats intensity. A Scottie's furnishings, the longer hair on the legs and underbody, and the beard tend to pick up debris and mat if neglected, so short, frequent brushing sessions are gentler on the dog and cheaper over time than occasional heavy detangling. If you plan to hand-strip, ask a groomer to show you the technique or plan to book it professionally on a regular cycle, because it is a learned skill and rushing it can be uncomfortable for the dog. Many owners settle on a hybrid: professional grooming on a schedule plus simple maintenance at home between visits.

Dental care for a small breed

Dental health is a lifelong, low-drama expense that pays off. The Merck Veterinary Manual explains that periodontal disease is the major reason for tooth loss in dogs, that small-breed dogs tend to have more problems with it than large breeds, and that gum disease will not develop around clean teeth. Merck recommends at-home care such as daily toothbrushing, with wiping the teeth every two to three days as a fallback, plus regular veterinary dental exams; it also cautions that human toothpaste should not be used.

Build a simple home routine and ask your vet how often professional cleaning is appropriate for your dog. Our small dog dental planning guide turns this into a schedule.

Merck also describes how periodontal disease progresses, noting that gingivitis, the earlier and reversible stage, is often first noticed around two years of age, while periodontitis, the irreversible stage that damages the tissues supporting the teeth, typically begins later and worsens if untreated. That timeline is useful for planning: the habits you build in a dog's first couple of years, when problems are still reversible, do the most good. Only brushing the outside surfaces of the teeth is needed, which makes the daily task quicker than many owners expect once the dog is comfortable with it.

Grooming-forward cost worksheet

BucketFormula to fill
SetupSlicker brush + comb + stripping tools or clippers + toothbrush and canine paste + crate
MonthlyFood (small-breed portion) + parasite prevention quote + at-home grooming supplies
GroomingProfessional groom quote x visits per year (hand-stripping typically more time than clipping)
Annual(Monthly x 12) + wellness exam + vaccines quote + budget line for veterinary dental care
ReserveEmergency fund target you can maintain for unexpected illness

Grooming is the row most people underestimate for this breed, so get a real quote before you decide.

A two-week grooming and training test

  1. Brushing habit: Brush a stuffed toy or practice the motions daily for two weeks; note whether you kept it up.
  2. Tooth handling: Practice the daily-brushing habit Merck recommends so it becomes routine, not a fight.
  3. Training patience: Run short, upbeat sessions and accept that an independent terrier sets its own pace.
  4. Groomer research: Call two groomers and ask about hand-stripping availability and pricing.

If daily upkeep felt like a chore in a low-stakes test, a real Scottie coat will be harder.

Questions for a breeder, rescue, or vet

The Orthopedic Foundation for Animals notes that a CHIC number means a dog completed its parent club's recommended screenings and released the results publicly, not that every result was normal.

  • Which health screenings does the breed club recommend, and can I see the parents' records?
  • How was the coat maintained, and do you recommend hand-stripping or clipping?
  • For a rescue: what is the dog's history with handling, grooming, and other pets?
  • For your vet: what home dental routine and cleaning schedule fit this small breed?

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Underbudgeting grooming. A harsh double coat needs regular professional work; price it before committing.
  • Skipping dental care. Merck notes small breeds are prone to periodontal disease; start home care early.
  • Expecting a pushover. The Diehard nickname is earned; train with patience and motivation.
  • Letting mats form. Regular brushing between grooms prevents painful, costly detangling.

A final quiet mistake is treating grooming as purely cosmetic. For this breed it is also comfort and skin health, so keeping the coat and skin clean and mat-free is part of care, not vanity, and it gives you regular chances to notice lumps or irritation to mention to your vet.

What this guide cannot tell you

It cannot quote your local groomer, predict your individual dog's temperament, or replace veterinary judgment. Merck's dental information is general education, not a diagnosis or treatment plan; only your veterinarian can examine your dog's mouth and recommend care. Use this to plan the grooming rhythm and the questions, then confirm prices and health specifics with the professionals you actually work with. Grooming quotes in particular vary widely by region and by whether you want hand-stripping, so two or three local calls will tell you far more than any national average ever could.

FAQ

Do Scottish Terriers need professional grooming?
Most owners rely on regular professional sessions plus at-home brushing. The harsh double coat can be hand-stripped to preserve texture or clipped for simplicity, and each choice affects your time and budget differently. Decide the method early, get a local quote, and keep up brushing between appointments so mats do not form and grooming stays manageable and affordable.
How important is dental care for this breed?
It is important. The Merck Veterinary Manual notes that periodontal disease is the leading cause of tooth loss in dogs and that small breeds are especially prone. Merck says gum disease will not develop around clean teeth, so start a home routine such as daily brushing early, use canine paste, and ask your vet how often professional cleaning is appropriate.
Are Scotties easy to train?
They are smart but independent. The AKC's Diehard nickname captures a dog that can be stubborn and self-directed. Training works best when it is short, positive, and motivating rather than repetitive drilling. Set realistic expectations for recall and off-leash reliability, and enjoy the spirited personality rather than fighting it into rigid obedience it may resist.
